module.title: Unit 5: Behavioral Economics & Cognitive Biases in Consumer Choice
module.objective: Mampu menganalisis bias kognitif (anchoring, loss aversion) dalam keputusan ekonomi menggunakan frasa akademis nuansatif.

subModules.title: Reading Mission: Why Prices Shape Our Choices
subModules.grammarFocus: Hedging and describing tendencies with tend to, be more likely to, and may be inclined to
subModules.vocabularyFocus: Cognitive biases, consumer decisions, pricing, and academic discussion

content.summary: In this reading mission, you will explore how cognitive biases can affect the way people judge prices and make buying decisions. You will read about anchoring, loss aversion, and the endowment effect, then use evidence from the text to explain these ideas. You will also practise describing common tendencies without claiming that they apply to everyone.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Use tend to + base verb to describe a general pattern, be more or less likely to + base verb to compare possibilities, and may or might be inclined to + base verb to present a cautious explanation.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Learn language for cognitive biases, consumer behavior, price comparisons, ownership, risk, and decision-making frameworks.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Skim each paragraph to identify its main point. Then scan for names, prices, comparisons, and explanations that support the main idea. Notice when the writer uses cautious language rather than making a claim about every person.

learningObjectives: Understand the main ideas in a B2 text about cognitive biases and consumer choice.
Locate details about how reference prices, possible losses, and ownership can influence decisions.
Recognize how examples support explanations of anchoring, loss aversion, and the endowment effect.
Use tend to, be more likely to, and may be inclined to describe patterns with appropriate caution.

contextWarmup.prompt: A shop displays a jacket with an original price of $200 and a sale price of $120. What might make the sale price seem especially attractive?
options: The original price may act as a reference point for judging the sale price.
The lower price proves that the jacket is better made.
Customers always prefer the first product they see.
contextWarmup.explanation: The original price can act as an anchor. Customers may compare the sale price with that first figure, even if they do not know the jacket's usual market value.

rules: Use subject + tend to + base verb to describe a common pattern, not a rule that is true of every person. For example: Shoppers tend to compare a sale price with the original price.
Use subject + be + more or less likely to + base verb when comparing the chance of an action in two situations. For example: People may be more likely to buy when a discount is shown clearly.
Use subject + may, might, or could + be inclined to + base verb to suggest a possible tendency. This wording is useful when discussing evidence that does not prove a claim about everyone.

commonTrap.explanation: A tendency is not the same as a certainty. Avoid changing a cautious claim about some consumers into a statement about all consumers.
commonTrap.wrong: Consumers always overvalue products they own.
commonTrap.correct: Consumers tend to place a higher value on products they own, although this tendency may not apply to everyone.

grammarFormulas.title: Sentence Patterns for Describing Consumer Tendencies
grammarFormulas.description: Assemble sentence blocks to practise general patterns, comparisons, and cautious explanations:

complements.text: a sale price with its original price

items.meaning: efek jangkar: kecenderungan mengandalkan informasi pertama saat membuat keputusan

items.meaning: aversi kerugian: kecenderungan lebih takut kehilangan daripada senang mendapat hal setara

items.collocation: a response shaped by loss aversion

items.meaning: bias kognitif: pola pikir sistematis yang menyimpang dari rasionalitas
items.exampleSentence: A cognitive bias can affect how a shopper interprets a discount.

items.meaning: efek endowment: kecenderungan menilai barang yang dimiliki lebih tinggi daripada barang serupa
items.exampleSentence: The endowment effect may explain why owners ask more for an item than buyers will pay.

items.meaning: kerangka pengambilan keputusan: struktur sistematis untuk menganalisis pilihan
items.exampleSentence: The researchers used a decision-making framework to compare consumer choices.

items.meaning: perilaku konsumen: cara individu membuat keputusan pembelian
items.exampleSentence: The study examined consumer behavior when products were offered at different prices.

items.meaning: harga acuan: harga yang digunakan sebagai pembanding
items.exampleSentence: A reference price can make a discount appear larger or smaller.

items.meaning: nilai yang dirasakan: penilaian seseorang terhadap manfaat atau harga suatu barang
items.exampleSentence: Clear information about quality can affect a customer's perceived value of a product.

items.meaning: kesediaan membayar: jumlah yang bersedia dibayarkan seseorang
items.exampleSentence: The survey measured customers' willingness to pay for a repair service.

items.meaning: pembingkaian harga: cara penyajian harga untuk memengaruhi penilaian
items.exampleSentence: Price framing can change how customers respond to the same offer.

paragraphs: When shoppers compare products, they do not always judge each option on its own. A first piece of information can shape the rest of the decision. Behavioral economists call this the anchoring effect. If a jacket is shown with an original price of $200 and a sale price of $120, the higher figure may become a reference point. The discount can then seem impressive, even when shoppers have not checked similar jackets elsewhere.

Anchors are not limited to shop labels. A suggested price, an online review, or the first offer in a negotiation can also influence a person's estimate. Consumers tend to rely more on an anchor when they have little time or limited knowledge. However, an anchor does not control every decision. A careful shopper may compare several products, check past prices, and ask whether the offer meets a real need.

Another pattern is loss aversion: people often react more strongly to a possible loss than to an equal-sized gain. For example, a customer might spend time and effort to avoid losing a discount that is about to expire, even if the purchase was not planned. Investors may also be inclined to hold onto a declining investment because selling would make the loss feel final. These are possible tendencies, not fixed rules.

Ownership can change how people judge value, too. The endowment effect describes the tendency to value an item more highly once it belongs to us. In one experiment, people who received a mug asked for more money to sell it than other participants were willing to pay to buy the same mug. The gap may reflect attachment and a stronger sense of loss at giving the mug up.

These ideas can help researchers build a decision-making framework that accounts for both prices and human reactions. They can also help shoppers pause before acting. One useful question is whether a price seems attractive because of its own quality and usefulness, or mainly because it is compared with a higher figure. This question does not remove bias, but it encourages a more considered choice.

Businesses can use what they know about consumer behavior when they present offers. That does not mean every price display is unfair, but it does make clear information important. A useful decision-making framework asks what information is being shown, what comparison it encourages, and whether customers can judge the offer easily. Shoppers are more likely to make informed choices when prices, conditions, and product details are presented plainly.

drills.instruction: Match each term with its meaning.

pairs.right: An early piece of information influences a later judgement.
A possible loss can feel stronger than an equal gain.
People may value something more once they own it.
A price used as a point of comparison.
The way a price is presented to customers.
The ways people make decisions about buying.

questions.question: What is the anchoring effect in the passage?
options: An early piece of information influences a later judgement.
People refuse to compare products.
Customers always buy the cheapest option.
questions.answer: An early piece of information influences a later judgement.
questions.explanation: The passage explains that a first figure, such as an original price, can shape how people judge a later price.

questions.question: Why might the $120 jacket seem like a particularly good deal?
options: The original $200 price may act as a reference point.
The passage says the jacket is made from better materials.
Customers have already checked every shop.
questions.answer: The original $200 price may act as a reference point.
questions.explanation: The higher original price can anchor shoppers, making the sale price seem impressive even without comparisons elsewhere.

questions.question: According to the passage, when may consumers rely more on an anchor?
options: When they have little time or limited knowledge.
Whenever they own the product.
Only when they shop online.
questions.answer: When they have little time or limited knowledge.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states that consumers tend to rely more on an anchor when they have little time or limited knowledge.

questions.question: What does loss aversion describe?
options: Reacting more strongly to a possible loss than to an equal-sized gain.
Preferring to buy products with a high original price.
Valuing every owned item at its market price.
questions.answer: Reacting more strongly to a possible loss than to an equal-sized gain.
questions.explanation: This is the definition given at the start of paragraph 3.

questions.question: Why might an investor hold onto a declining investment?
options: Selling may make the loss feel final.
The investment is certain to recover.
Investors do not compare financial risks.
questions.answer: Selling may make the loss feel final.
questions.explanation: The passage says investors may be inclined to keep a declining investment because selling would make the loss feel final.

questions.question: What did the mug experiment illustrate?
options: Owners asked for more to sell the mug than other participants would pay to buy it.
Every participant valued the mug at the same price.
People preferred mugs to other products.
questions.answer: Owners asked for more to sell the mug than other participants would pay to buy it.
questions.explanation: The difference between the owners' asking price and the buyers' willingness to pay illustrates the endowment effect.

questions.question: What may explain the gap between the sellers' and buyers' prices for the mug?
options: Attachment and a stronger sense of loss at giving it up.
The mug's original shop price.
A lack of information about online reviews.
questions.answer: Attachment and a stronger sense of loss at giving it up.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 suggests that attachment and the feeling of losing the mug may contribute to the gap.

questions.question: What question does the passage suggest shoppers ask about an attractive price?
options: Is it attractive because of its quality and usefulness, or mainly because it is compared with a higher figure?
Was it the first product displayed in the shop?
Will the price remain unchanged forever?
questions.answer: Is it attractive because of its quality and usefulness, or mainly because it is compared with a higher figure?
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 recommends separating the product's own value from the effect of comparison with a higher price.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the writer's view of price displays?
options: Not every price display is unfair, but clear information matters.
All businesses use prices to mislead customers.
Price displays have no effect on consumer choices.
questions.answer: Not every price display is unfair, but clear information matters.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph says that businesses may use what they know about consumer behavior, while also stressing the importance of clear information.

questions.question: Why does the writer use phrases such as tend to and may be inclined to?
options: To describe possible patterns without claiming they apply to everyone.
To show that the ideas have no supporting examples.
To suggest that consumers always behave irrationally.
questions.answer: To describe possible patterns without claiming they apply to everyone.
questions.explanation: The passage calls these tendencies, not fixed rules, and uses cautious language to avoid making absolute claims.

subModules.title: Listening Mission: Behavioral Economics in Action

content.summary: This briefing prepares you to follow rapid academic discussions about behavioral economics. You will learn how to detect key bias concepts, recognize attitude shifts, and interpret connected speech patterns commonly heard in university study discussions.
learningObjectives: Identify explicit definitions and real-world examples of cognitive biases in casual conversation.
Distinguish between buyer reactions to anchoring and seller behavior driven by loss aversion.
Catch intrusive glides and consonant linking in rapid conversational exchanges.

keyPhrases.meaning: efek jangkar (ketergantungan berlebih pada angka awal)
keyPhrases.note: Used to describe how people rely heavily on the first piece of information offered.
Refers to the psychological tendency to prefer avoiding losses over acquiring equivalent gains.

keyPhrases.meaning: terpaku atau memegang teguh pada sesuatu
keyPhrases.note: Informal phrasal verb meaning to fixate quickly on an idea, number, or concept.
A customer's subjective evaluation of the merit or worth of a good or service.

connectedSpeech.note: Consonant-to-vowel linking connects the final /k/ of 'look' directly to the unstressed /ə/ in 'at'.
An intrusive glide /j/ bridges the diphthong /aɪ/ and the following vowel /ɒ/.
The final /t/ in 'reject' is elided before the consonant /r/ in casual speech.
The final /s/ links fluidly with the short vowel /ɪ/ in the particle 'in'.

content.context: Alex and Morgan are reviewing research findings in the library before their behavioral economics seminar.

lines.text: What about the sellers this time?

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Analysing Bias in Consumer Choice

content.summary: Use cautious academic language to describe patterns in consumer decisions without suggesting that every person behaves in the same way. Explain a bias, give evidence or an example, and show how it may influence a choice. Use tendency phrases to describe general patterns, likelihood phrases to compare situations, and modal verbs to present a possible explanation.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Describe a General Tendency
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + tend(s) to + base verb / tend(s) to be + adjective
blueprintItems.example: Consumers tend to overvalue products that they already own.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Compare Likelihood
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + be + more/less likely to + base verb
blueprintItems.example: Shoppers are more likely to choose a product when its discount is shown beside a higher original price.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Present a Cautious Explanation
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + may/might/could + be + inclined to + base verb
blueprintItems.example: Investors may be inclined to keep a losing stock because selling it would make the loss feel final.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use a singular verb after a singular subject with tend, and use the base verb after tend to.
mechanicsRules.badExample: A shopper tend to prefer the first price they see.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: A shopper tends to prefer the first price they see.
mechanicsRules.why: In the present simple, a third-person singular subject takes a verb ending in -s. The verb after to stays in its base form.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use be before more or less likely, and use the base form of the next verb after to.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Consumers more likely to notice a price increase.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Consumers are more likely to notice a price increase.
mechanicsRules.why: Likely is an adjective, so it needs a form of be. The following verb is the base form after to.

mechanicsRules.rule: Place may, might, or could before be, and use the base form of the main verb after inclined to.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Buyers might are inclined to avoid a perceived loss.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Buyers might be inclined to avoid a perceived loss.
mechanicsRules.why: A modal verb is followed by the base form of be. In this pattern, the main verb follows to in its base form.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 1: Explain an Anchor Price
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write four to five sentences explaining how an initial price might influence a shopper's choice. Include one tendency phrase, one example, and a cautious statement that avoids claiming all shoppers behave in the same way.
guidedLabChallenges.example: Shoppers tend to notice the first price displayed for a product. This price can act as an anchor when they consider a later discount. For example, a reduced price may seem attractive beside a much higher original price. However, shoppers may also compare prices across different stores.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 2: Discuss Loss Aversion
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write four to five sentences about how fear of a loss could affect a consumer or investor. Compare two situations or groups using more or less likely, and support your point with a reason or example.
guidedLabChallenges.example: Investors may be inclined to keep shares whose value has fallen. Selling them can make the loss feel certain, while holding them leaves open the possibility of recovery. Investors may be less likely to sell when they focus on the purchase price. This response can vary according to a person's goals and knowledge.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using tend to while keeping the meaning.
practicumQuestions.promptText: Many shoppers often rely on the first price they see.
targetAnswers: Many shoppers tend to rely on the first price they see.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Tend to describes a common pattern without suggesting that it happens in every case.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using more likely to.
practicumQuestions.promptText: A shopper has a greater chance of choosing a product when the discount is clear.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use the pattern: A shopper is more likely to...
targetAnswers: A shopper is more likely to choose a product when the discount is clear.
practicumQuestions.explanation: More likely to compares the probability of an action in a particular situation.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using may be inclined to.
practicumQuestions.promptText: Investors might keep losing shares because selling them makes the loss feel final.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use may be inclined to followed by a base verb.
targetAnswers: Investors may be inclined to keep losing shares because selling them makes the loss feel final.
practicumQuestions.explanation: May presents a possible explanation, while be inclined to describes a tendency to act in a particular way.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Join the ideas using although to show contrast.
practicumQuestions.promptText: The original price can act as an anchor. It does not control every shopper's choice.
practicumQuestions.hint: Place although at the beginning of the sentence and use a comma between the clauses.
targetAnswers: Although the original price can act as an anchor, it does not control every shopper's choice.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Although introduces information that contrasts with the main clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the sentence with a conjunction that gives a reason.
practicumQuestions.promptText: Some consumers keep unwanted items ______ returning them feels like a loss.
practicumQuestions.hint: Choose a conjunction that means 'for the reason that'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Because introduces the reason why some consumers keep the items.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Join the ideas using whereas to compare two groups.
practicumQuestions.promptText: Some shoppers focus on the sale price. Other shoppers compare the product across several stores.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use whereas between the two contrasting clauses.
targetAnswers: Some shoppers focus on the sale price, whereas other shoppers compare the product across several stores.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Whereas connects two contrasting patterns or groups.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the capitalization, verb form, and punctuation.
practicumQuestions.promptText: a consumer tend to remember the first price
practicumQuestions.hint: Use tends with a singular subject and add a full stop.
targetAnswers: A consumer tends to remember the first price.
practicumQuestions.explanation: A singular subject takes tends in the present simple. Begin with a capital letter and end the sentence with a full stop.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the sentence.
practicumQuestions.promptText: buyers are more likely choosing a product with a visible discount
practicumQuestions.hint: Use the base verb after likely to.
targetAnswers: Buyers are more likely to choose a product with a visible discount.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The pattern is be more likely to followed by the base form of the verb.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write one sentence explaining how anchoring might affect a shopper. Use tend to and give a relevant example.
practicumQuestions.promptText: How could an initial price influence a later purchase decision?
practicumQuestions.hint: Describe a general tendency, then refer to an original or sale price.
targetAnswers: Shoppers tend to compare a sale price with the first price they saw, so that initial price may act as an anchor.
Consumers tend to use an original price as a reference point when deciding whether a discount seems attractive.
practicumQuestions.explanation: A strong response uses tend to for a general pattern and connects the initial price to a later judgement.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write two sentences about loss aversion. Use may, might, or could be inclined to, and avoid making an absolute claim.
practicumQuestions.promptText: Why might an investor keep a losing investment?
practicumQuestions.hint: Mention that selling can make a loss feel certain, but acknowledge that decisions can differ.
targetAnswers: Investors may be inclined to keep losing shares because selling them can make the loss feel final. However, this response may differ according to their goals and circumstances.
An investor might be inclined to hold a losing investment because selling it makes the loss feel real. Not every investor responds in the same way.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Modal verbs make the explanation cautious, and the second sentence prevents an unsupported claim about all investors.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Biases in Consumer Choice

content.summary: Explain how cognitive biases can shape consumer choices. Use precise vocabulary and cautious academic phrases such as “This may suggest that…” and “One possible explanation is…”. Support claims with examples rather than presenting them as universal truths.
content.audioGuidance: Give key terms clear stress, especially ANCHoring effect and loss aVERsion. Pause briefly before examples and contrast words such as “initially” and “ultimately”. Use a falling tone for conclusions and a rising tone when asking genuine questions.

pillars.name: Vowel Clarity
pillars.target: Clear vowels in key economics terms
pillars.explanation: Keep the vowel sounds distinct in “loss”, “choice”, and “effect”. Avoid rushing through longer words such as “consumer” and “decision-making”.

pillars.name: Word Stress
pillars.explanation: Stress the first syllable in “cognitive” and “consumer”, and the second syllable in “behavior”. Clear stress helps listeners recognise academic terms.

pillars.name: Nuanced Delivery
pillars.explanation: Use phrases such as “to some extent” and “it could be argued that” to show appropriate caution. Follow each claim with a specific consumer example.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: The stress falls on the first syllable in “anchoring” but on the second syllable in “aversion”.
“Cognitive” has first-syllable stress, while “behavior” has second-syllable stress.
Both words have three syllables, but “endowment” stresses the second syllable and “consumer” stresses the second syllable with a different vowel sound.
“Framework” is stressed on the first syllable, while “decision” is stressed on the second.

drills.targetText: The anchoring effect can make an initial price seem more reasonable.
drills.phonetic: /ði ˈæŋkərɪŋ ɪˈfekt kən meɪk ən ɪˈnɪʃəl praɪs siːm mɔː ˈriːzənəbəl/
drills.focus: Word stress in “anchoring effect” and clear linking
drills.hint: Stress the first syllable in “anchoring” and the second syllable in “effect”.

drills.targetText: Loss aversion may explain why some shoppers avoid a risky purchase.
drills.phonetic: /lɒs əˈvɜːʃən meɪ ɪkˈspleɪn waɪ sʌm ˈʃɒpəz əˈvɔɪd ə ˈrɪski ˈpɜːtʃəs/
drills.focus: Stress in “aversion” and cautious academic phrasing
drills.hint: Give “VER” in “aversion” the main stress, then keep the rest of the sentence measured.

drills.targetText: The endowment effect may lead owners to value their belongings more highly.
drills.phonetic: /ði ɪnˈdaʊmənt ɪˈfekt meɪ liːd ˈəʊnəz tə ˈvæljuː ðeə bəˈlɒŋɪŋz mɔː ˈhaɪli/
drills.focus: Clear syllables in “endowment” and sentence rhythm
drills.hint: Stress the second syllable in “endowment” and pause lightly before the explanation.

drills.targetText: A decision-making framework can help us analyse consumer behavior.
drills.phonetic: /ə dɪˈsɪʒən ˌmeɪkɪŋ ˈfreɪmwɜːk kən help ʌs ˈænəlaɪz kənˈsjuːmə bɪˈheɪvjə/
drills.hint: Make “framework” and “behavior” easy to distinguish by stressing their correct syllables.

roleplay.context: You are discussing a promotional offer with a consumer researcher. The offer lists a high original price beside a lower sale price, and the researcher asks how this presentation might affect shoppers.

turns.speaker: Consumer Researcher
turns.text: The price was first shown as $500 and then reduced to $350. What effect might the original price have?
turns.translation: Harga pertama kali ditampilkan sebesar $500, lalu diturunkan menjadi $350. Apa pengaruh harga awal tersebut?

turns.speaker: Student
turns.text: It could create an anchoring effect, so shoppers may judge the reduced price in relation to the original one.
turns.translation: Hal itu dapat menciptakan efek jangkar, sehingga pembeli mungkin menilai harga diskon dengan membandingkannya dengan harga awal.

turns.speaker: Consumer Researcher
turns.text: Could loss aversion also influence whether someone accepts this offer?
turns.translation: Apakah aversi kerugian juga dapat memengaruhi keputusan seseorang untuk menerima tawaran ini?

turns.speaker: Student
turns.text: Possibly. A shopper might worry about missing the discount, although we would need evidence to know how much that matters.
turns.translation: Mungkin. Pembeli bisa khawatir kehilangan kesempatan mendapat diskon, meskipun kita memerlukan bukti untuk mengetahui seberapa besar pengaruhnya.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Speak for at least 30 seconds about a purchase you made after seeing an original price and a sale price.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Describe the purchase and explain whether the first price affected your decision.
storyPoints: What the item was and what prices you saw
How you compared the original price with the sale price
Whether you bought it and what you think influenced your choice
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The original price may have created an anchoring effect, although I also considered whether I needed the item.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ði əˈrɪdʒənəl praɪs meɪ hæv kriˈeɪtɪd ən ˈæŋkərɪŋ ɪˈfekt/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Tell the story in a clear sequence and use cautious language when explaining what may have influenced you.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Speak for at least 30 seconds about a time you or someone you know held onto, or avoided giving up, something valuable.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Describe what happened and discuss whether loss aversion or the endowment effect could help explain the choice.
storyPoints: What item, investment, or decision was involved
What the person might have feared losing or valued because it was already theirs
What alternative choice was available and what lesson you draw from the example
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Loss aversion might explain the reluctance to sell, while the endowment effect could also have affected the item's perceived value.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /lɒs əˈvɜːʃən maɪt ɪkˈspleɪn ðə rɪˈlʌktəns tə sel/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Distinguish the possible explanations and avoid claiming that one bias definitely caused the decision.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Take part in a live call. Explain how a displayed original price might shape a shopper's judgement, then answer the researcher's follow-up question.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: A researcher is interviewing you about a product advertised as reduced from $500 to $350.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are a consumer interviewed by a researcher about a discounted product. Discuss how seeing the original price first might affect your judgement, while also considering the item's usefulness.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are the interviewee. Give a balanced answer and ask the researcher one relevant question.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Seeing $500 first could create an anchoring effect, but I would also consider the product's quality and whether I need it.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Respond directly, give at least one reason, and use “could” or “might” to express uncertainty.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Take part in a live call. Discuss why an investor might keep a falling investment and suggest what further information would help explain the choice.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: A researcher asks whether fear of a loss can affect investment decisions.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are speaking to a behavioral economics researcher about an investor who refuses to sell a declining stock. Explore possible reasons without assuming that the investor's choice has only one cause.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a research participant with a basic understanding of behavioral economics. Explain how loss aversion might apply and ask what other factors the researcher is considering.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Loss aversion could play a part, although the investor's goals and financial situation may also matter.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Offer a plausible explanation, acknowledge other factors, and keep your tone analytical.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Take part in a live call. Explain why an owner might ask more for an item than another person would pay, and respond to a question about how to test this idea.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: A researcher is studying why people sometimes value their own belongings highly.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are discussing a second-hand bicycle with a researcher. The owner asks more than similar bicycles usually sell for and says the bicycle is especially valuable to them.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are the interviewee. Connect the example to the endowment effect, but recognise that condition and personal attachment could also matter.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The endowment effect may lead the owner to value the bicycle more highly, but its condition could also explain the price.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Apply the concept to the example and offer another reasonable explanation.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Take part in a live call. Describe a simple framework for analysing a purchase and explain how it could help someone notice a bias.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: A researcher asks how consumers could make more considered decisions.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You and a researcher are discussing a shopper choosing between two phones. The shopper feels pressured by a limited-time discount and is unsure whether to buy.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are the interviewee. Suggest a practical decision-making framework, including a pause to compare needs, costs, and alternatives.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: A decision-making framework could help the shopper compare the total cost and their actual needs before deciding.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Set out your steps in a logical order and explain how they might reduce the influence of pressure.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Define “anchoring effect”, “loss aversion”, and “consumer behavior” in your own words. Give one short consumer example for each term.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Explain three key terms and use each in a sentence.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Loss aversion describes a tendency to fear a loss more than to value an equivalent gain.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Show that you understand each term by giving a clear definition and an appropriate example.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Use “may”, “might”, and “could” to make three cautious claims about how cognitive biases can affect a consumer's choice.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Make three possible explanations without presenting them as certain facts.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: An initial price might influence a shopper, and loss aversion could make a discount feel difficult to refuse.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use modal verbs accurately to distinguish a possible explanation from a proven cause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say “anchoring effect”, “cognitive bias”, “endowment effect”, and “consumer behavior”. Emphasise the stressed syllables clearly.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Pronounce each phrase at a steady pace, then use one phrase in a short sentence.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The anchoring effect may influence consumer behavior.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ði ˈæŋkərɪŋ ɪˈfekt meɪ ˈɪnfluəns kənˈsjuːmə bɪˈheɪvjə/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Keep the main stress clear: first syllable in “anchoring” and “cognitive”, second syllable in “effect”, “endowment”, and “behavior”.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say one genuine yes-or-no question with rising intonation, then give a reasoned conclusion with falling intonation about a consumer choice.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Ask whether an initial price can influence a decision, then state what you think the shopper should consider.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Could the first price influence the shopper? They should also compare the product's cost with their needs.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Let your voice rise naturally at the end of the genuine question and fall at the end of your complete statement.
